title: Factories and a component, generated at build time
goal: By the end you can say what dependency injection does, write a KSP processor that generates a factory for each @Inject class and a component that builds the whole graph in dependency order, and compare it with a container that wires by reflection.
opening:
Picture moving day at a family's house. The truck needs a driver, the driver needs the route, and every packer needs a roll of tape. The crew can't start until the truck and the packers are ready. Someone has to work out the order, and what is shared: one truck for the whole day, but a new roll of tape for each packer.

You can write that plan the night before, or work it out on the street at seven in the morning, with the crew waiting and the meter running. In Part 4's capstone you built a small dependency injection container, a program that builds your objects and hands each one what its constructor asks for. It did the second: it read your classes by reflection every time the program started. The last lesson, Choosing the tool, weighed reflection against KSP.

In this capstone we'll write the plan the night before. In this sitting, a KSP processor writes one factory per class, then a component that builds the whole crew in the right order. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A generated component builds `Route`, then `Driver(route)`, then `Truck(driver)`, each as a `private val` in a Kotlin class. What happens if the generator writes the driver's line above the route's?
options: Nothing changes: Kotlin initializes properties in any order it likes
It compiles, and the driver gets `null` for its route at run time
It doesn't compile: Kotlin rejects an initializer that reads a property declared below it
KSP sorts the lines before the compiler sees them
warmup.why: Kotlin runs property initializers from top to bottom, and the compiler refuses one that reads a property declared further down: `Variable 'route' must be initialized.` (javac says `illegal forward reference` for the Java version). So the generator must write the plan in dependency order, which is the walk in the third section. The `null` answer is tempting because a call through a function can sneak past the check; a direct read can't.

sections.h: The night before or on the street: generated wiring next to the reflection container
sections.body:
Both ways build the same crew. They differ in when the work happens and in what you see when it goes wrong. Here's the generated component next to Part 4's reflection container:

| | Reflection container (Part 4) | Generated component (this lesson) |
|---|---|---|
| When the wiring is checked | When the program first asks for a part | When the build runs |
| What runs at start | Reading annotations, `getConstructors()` and `newInstance` for every part | One constructor call per part, in order |
| What you can read | Nothing: the plan exists only in memory | A Kotlin file in `build/generated/ksp` |
| A mistake looks like | An exception thrown from inside the container | An error on the file and line of your class |
| Can it change its mind at run time? | Yes: it can scan for parts and choose | No: the plan is fixed when you build |

Let the build settle the fourth row. Delete `@Inject` from `Driver` in `app/src/l01` and run `./gradlew :injector:app:kspL01Kotlin`:

```text
e: [ksp] .../labs/injector/app/src/l01/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l01/Truck.kt:8: Truck needs Driver, but nobody provides Driver. Add @Inject to its constructor.

> Task :injector:app:kspL01Kotlin FAILED
   > KSP failed with exit code: PROCESSING_ERROR
```

The program never ran. The error points at line 8 of `Truck.kt`, where the truck asks for a driver, and not at a line of the processor. In a reflection container, the same mistake would surface only when the app first asked for the crew, as an exception from the container's own code. The next lesson shows that stack trace. A stack trace from a reflection container is mostly the container talking about itself.

Using the generated component is ordinary code in either language. It compiles to a plain class, so Java calls it like any other:

```java
MovingDayComponent plan = new GeneratedMovingDayComponent();
MovingDay day = plan.movingDay();
System.out.println(plan.truck() == day.getCrew().getTruck());   // true: one truck
```

```kotlin
val plan: MovingDayComponent = GeneratedMovingDayComponent()
val day = plan.movingDay()
println(plan.truck() === day.crew.truck)                           // true: one truck
```

**Wiring that depends only on your classes can be checked when you build. Check it there.**

The last row of the table is the price. The generated plan can't discover a part while the program runs, or choose one from a setting, unless the build wrote code for it. Today's processor has three gaps of its own, too. Its message names only the last step ("Truck needs Driver"), which helps little when ten classes need a driver. It has no answer to a cycle. And it has no way to bind a class you can't put a note on, such as one from a library. Those three are the next lesson.

try.title: Forget a note, and see who complains
steps: In `labs/injector/app/src/l01/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l01/Driver.kt`, delete `@Inject`. From `labs/`, run `./gradlew :injector:app:kspL01Kotlin`. Which file and line does the error name, and why that one?
Now put the note on the class instead (`@Inject class Driver(val route: Route) { ... }`, keeping `@Singleton` above it) and run the task again.
Open `GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt` once more. Did anything in it change?
try.expect: The first run fails with `e: [ksp] .../Truck.kt:8: Truck needs Driver, but nobody provides Driver. Add @Inject to its constructor.` and `KSP failed with exit code: PROCESSING_ERROR`: the error names the truck's parameter, where a driver is asked for. With `@Inject` on the class, the build passes, `DriverFactory.kt` is back, and the component is the same as before, because a note on the class means its primary constructor.

compare.title: One card, two helpers: the factory javac's processor writes and the one KSP writes

java.title: DriverFactory.java (from FactoryDemoJava)

kotlin.title: DriverFactory.kt (from FactoryDemo)

compare.note: Both helpers read the same constructor and write a card that takes what it takes and calls it. The Java card is a final class with a static method and a private constructor, so nobody can build the factory itself; the Kotlin card is an `object`, which Java reaches through `INSTANCE`. The javac processor wrote its text with a string template, so it spells `movemate.Route` in full; KotlinPoet manages imports and would add one for a type from another package. Neither card uses reflection, and both are ordinary source that the compiler checks like your own.

worked.title: Add a moving blanket to the plan

steps.say: The family's piano needs wrapping, so a packer now needs a moving blanket. Start with the class, and give it an `@Inject` constructor.
Ask for it where it's needed: in the packer's constructor. That's the only change you make by hand.
steps.code:
@Inject
class Packer(val tape: TapeRoll, val blanket: Blanket)

steps.say: Build. KSP writes `BlanketFactory`, `PackerFactory.create` gains a parameter, and the packer's line in the component changes. The walk put the blanket before the packer, as post-order must.
steps.code:
private fun newBlanket(): Blanket = BlanketFactory.create()

private fun newPacker(): Packer = PackerFactory.create(newTapeRoll(), newBlanket())
steps.alt_code:
private Blanket newBlanket() { return BlanketFactory.create(); }

private Packer newPacker() { return PackerFactory.create(newTapeRoll(), newBlanket()); }

steps.say: Decide whether it's shared. Without `@Singleton`, each packer gets its own blanket, like its own roll of tape. Add `@Singleton` only if one blanket for the whole day is what you mean, because then every packer wraps with the same one.

lab.title: Write the factory processor and the component processor
steps: Run the tests once. Five of seven fail, each with a warning such as `w: [ksp] l01 not done yet: write <Name>Factory.kt: ...`. The two that pass test the given checks. The crew the tests compile is in `src/test/kotlin/workbench/injector/l01/MoveMateSources.kt`.

Find and Check are given. Read `writeFactories` and `checked` in `FactoryProcessor.kt`, then `writeComponents` and `checkedEntryPoints` in `ComponentProcessor.kt`. Note which `Dependencies` each processor passes, and why.

Write: in `factoryFile`, build one `ParameterSpec` per constructor parameter (`it.type.toTypeName()`), a `create` function that returns `%T(%L)`, and an `objectBuilder` around it. Run `FactoriesTest` until its three tests pass.

Read: in `Bindings.kt`, write `creationOrder`. Walk depth first from each entry point, add a binding when you leave it, and add each one once. For a type nobody provides, log the exact message from the KDoc on the parameter that asks, keep walking, and return null at the end.

Write: in `componentFile`, add a `PropertySpec` for each singleton in the order you're given, a private `FunSpec` for each of the others, then one override per entry point. Use `memberName`, `reference` and `construct`.

Prove: run the tests until all seven pass. Then run your processors in the real build with `./gradlew :injector:app:kspL01Kotlin -Pmine=l01`, open the generated component, and run `./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l01.MovingDayAppKt -Pmine=l01`.
From memory: close the files and write the post-order walk on paper, for a map from each class name to the names it needs. Then compare it with your `creationOrder`.
hints: `binding.parameters` works for both kinds of note: `checked` already found the constructor, whether `@Inject` sat on the class or on the constructor.
`parameters.map { CodeBlock.of("%N", it) }.joinToCode(", ")` gives `truck, kitchenPacker, bedroomPacker` for the constructor call.

If a test prints `Variable 'route' must be initialized.`, your component lists a singleton before something it needs. The order from `creationOrder` must be post-order: a binding goes in after its dependencies.
KotlinPoet writes all properties before all functions, whatever order you add them in. That's why the vals come first in the file, and why the private functions can be added in any order.
lab.done_when: All seven tests in `FactoriesTest` and `ComponentTest` pass, and `MovingDayApp` prints `one truck for the whole day: true` with `-Pmine=l01`.

drill.title: Write the creation order from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `creationOrder(needs, wanted)`: `needs` maps each class name to the names its constructor asks for, and the result lists every name the `wanted` ones need, each after everything it needs, each once. Check it on `MovingDay -> [Crew, Route]`, `Crew -> [Truck, Packer]`, `Truck -> [Driver]`, `Driver -> [Route]`, `Packer -> [TapeRoll]`, wanting `[MovingDay]`. Then write it in Java.

alt.title: CreationOrder.java

recap: Dependency injection hands each object what its constructor asks for. A binding says how to get one type; a singleton exists once per plan, and anything else is built new for each request.
The factory processor writes one `<Name>Factory` per `@Inject` class: an isolating output, written with `Dependencies(aggregating = false, thatClassFile)`.

The component processor walks the graph depth first from the `@Component` functions and writes the plan in post-order: a `private val` per singleton, a `new...()` function for the rest, an override per entry point.
The order is load-bearing: Kotlin rejects an initializer that reads a property declared below it (`Variable 'route' must be initialized.`), and javac does the same (`illegal forward reference`).
The component is aggregating: built from many files and redone whenever any of them changes. A mistake in the wiring fails the build on the file and line that asked.
The limit: the plan is fixed when you build, the message names only the last step, and the walk has no memory of its path, so a cycle runs it until the stack runs out.
closing:
We started with a moving-day plan that someone has to write before the crew arrives. KSP now writes it during the build: a factory for each class, the isolating cards, and a component that builds the crew in dependency order, the aggregating master list. One truck, one route, two rolls of tape, and no reflection anywhere.

In your own code, find the block near `main` that calls `new` on helper after helper. That block is a hand-written plan.

Next, we'll break the plan on purpose: a driver nobody provides, a driver who waits for the truck, and two routes with no names. Can the build name every mistake, with its file and line, before anyone moves a box?

quiz.q: The factory processor writes `DriverFactory.kt` from the `@Inject` constructor in `Driver.kt`. Which `Dependencies` should it pass?
options: `Dependencies(aggregating = false, driverFile)`
`Dependencies(aggregating = true, driverFile)`
`Dependencies.ALL_FILES`
`Dependencies(false)`, with no files
quiz.why: The card depends on `Driver.kt` alone, so it's isolating and names that file. Aggregating would redo it whenever any file changes, and `ALL_FILES` switches incremental processing off. With no files at all, KSP can't tie the output to a source, and an incremental build can delete it as a stale output, the trap from Incremental builds and processor options.

quiz.q: `Packer` has no `@Singleton`, and `Crew @Inject constructor(val truck: Truck, val kitchenPacker: Packer, val bedroomPacker: Packer)` is a singleton. How many tape rolls does one component make for its crew?
options: One, shared by both packers
Two, one for each packer
None until a packer uses one
It depends on the order of the constructor parameters
quiz.why: The crew's line calls `newPacker()` twice, and every call builds a new packer with a new tape roll from `newTapeRoll()`. A roll would be shared only if `TapeRoll` were a singleton. The crew itself is built once, so the count stays at two however often you ask for the moving day.

quiz.q: `Truck` loses its `@Singleton`; everything else stays the same. What does `plan.truck() === plan.movingDay().crew.truck` print?
options: `true`, because the crew is a singleton
A compile error in the generated component
The generated code throws at run time
`false`
quiz.why: The truck becomes `private fun newTruck()`. The crew, still a singleton, got a truck when it was built, and `truck()` now builds another one. Both compile and run fine; they're just two trucks. The demo in the second Try it prints exactly that.

quiz.q: `Driver` has no `@Inject`, and `Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver)` asks for one. Where does lesson 1's error point?
options: At the processor's own source code
At the generated component
At `Truck.kt`, on the line of `val driver: Driver`
At `Driver.kt`, on the class line
quiz.why: The walk reports a missing binding on the parameter that asks for it, with `logger.error(message, parameter)`. That's the place you'd look first: the request nobody can answer. The generated component isn't written at all when the walk finds a problem.

quiz.q: Which job could Part 4's reflection container do that the generated component can't?
options: Share one instance among many classes
Pick a part it finds on the class path while the program runs
Build parts in dependency order
Report a missing binding
quiz.why: The generated plan is fixed when you build: it can only build what the processor wrote code for. Both can share singletons, order the graph and report a missing binding; the generated one just does the last two in the build, before the program runs.

flashcards.back: An object another object needs to do its job. The driver is a dependency of the truck.
A class lists what it needs as constructor parameters, and something outside builds those and passes them in.

flashcards.front: Isolating or aggregating: a factory for one `@Inject` class?
flashcards.back: Isolating. It depends only on that class's file: `Dependencies(aggregating = false, file)`.

flashcards.front: Isolating or aggregating: the generated component?
flashcards.back: Aggregating. It's built from many files and is redone whenever any of them changes.

flashcards.front: In what order does the component build its singletons, and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: Depth-first post-order: each one after everything its constructor needs. Kotlin initializes properties top to bottom and rejects a forward read with `Variable '...' must be initialized.`

flashcards.front: How does the generated component handle a binding without `@Singleton`?
flashcards.back: As a private `new<Name>()` function, so every request builds a new object.

terms.plain: An object that another object needs in order to do its job.
Handing an object its dependencies from outside, instead of letting it build them itself.
Dependency injection through constructor parameters: the class says what it needs, and someone else passes it in.
One line of the plan: how to get one type, such as "call the @Inject constructor of Driver".
A binding that exists once per component and is shared by everyone who asks for it.
The bindings and the arrows between them: who needs whom.
Generated code whose only job is to build one class from what its constructor takes.
The generated class that implements a @Component interface and builds the whole graph in dependency order.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate opens `GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt` and asks three things: what this class is for, why its lines come in exactly that order, and why KSP is told different things about the factories and about the component. Explain.
explain_back.answer: It's the plan for the moving day, written by a processor during the build. Each class says in its constructor what it needs, and the component builds everything the `MovingDayComponent` interface hands out, handing each class its dependencies. Singletons, like the one truck, are private vals built once; everything else, like a tape roll, comes from a private function, so each request gets a new one. The lines are in depth-first post-order: every val comes after the vals it reads. Kotlin initializes properties from top to bottom and won't compile a line that reads a property declared below it, so the order is what makes the class compile at all. Each factory depends only on its own class's file, so it's declared isolating, and KSP can leave it alone when another file changes. The component is built from many files, so it's declared aggregating and is redone whenever any file changes.

deeper.body:
Why generate factories at all, when the component could call each constructor directly? In a single module, it could. The factory earns its keep when classes live in several modules. A library module compiled earlier ships its factories with it, and the component in the app module only calls them. Each factory is compiled once, in the module that owns the class, so the app's build never needs to look inside that class's constructor again beyond its signature.

Our component builds its singletons eagerly, in the constructor. That keeps the generated text in plain dependency order, and it's thread-safe for a simple reason: each `private val` compiles to a `private final` field, and the memory model guarantees that final fields set in a constructor are visible to any thread that sees the finished object (the memory model track has the rule). The cost is that creating the component builds everything, even parts nobody asks for. Lesson 3 adds `Lazy<T>` for the one expensive part.

A singleton here is one per component object, not one per program. Create two `GeneratedMovingDayComponent`s and you get two trucks. That's usually what you want in tests: each test builds its own plan.

The javac twin of the factory processor has a trap of its own. Since JDK 23, javac doesn't run processors it merely finds on the class path; it needs `--processor-path`, `-processor` or `-proc:full`. Gradle's `annotationProcessor` configuration passes the processor path explicitly, and `FactoryDemoJava` hands the processor to the compiler task directly, so neither is affected.
